title_en: Homily on the Parable of the Vineyard
author: Cyril of Alexandria
addressee: a Christian congregation or reader addressed as 'beloved'
occasion: Cyril expounds the Gospel parable of the laborers in the vineyard, interpreting its details for the spiritual benefit of his hearers.
argument: Cyril interprets the parable of the vineyard allegorically. The householder is God, the vineyard is human nature, and the laborers are the saints who serve human salvation. The successive hours of hiring represent the ages of salvation history: Abel, Enoch, and Noah; Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; Moses and Aaron under the law; the prophets; and finally the coming of Christ. The idle laborers hired at the eleventh hour are the Gentiles, who had been without the law and the prophets. The Church, once idle, now works through apostles, martyrs, ascetics, monastics, virgins, the self-controlled, and the married, and receives the denarius worthily; the repentant thief shows that one hour of swift work can equal a full day's labor.

outline.move: Cyril introduces the parable and begins decoding its figures: the householder is God, the world is his house, the vineyard is human nature, and the laborers are the saints.
He maps the hours of the day onto salvation history from Abel through the law of Moses and the prophets up to the coming of Christ.
He identifies the idle laborers hired at the eleventh hour as the Gentiles, who had been without knowledge of God, law, or prophets.
He describes the Church's present labor, cites the repentant thief as an example of swift work, and recounts the earlier laborers' complaint and the householder's response that he does them no wrong.

cast.name: God
cast.who: The creator and master of the world, represented by the householder in the parable.

cast.name: Abel
cast.who: An early righteous man, counted among the first laborers of the vineyard.

cast.name: Enoch
cast.who: An early righteous man, counted among the first laborers of the vineyard.

cast.name: Noah
cast.who: An early righteous man; Cyril says he planted a vineyard but immediately adds 'understand this spiritually,' so the reference is to a spiritual meaning, not literal Noah.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.who: Patriarch whose era is the second period of laborers.

cast.name: Isaac
cast.who: Patriarch whose era is the second period of laborers.

cast.name: Jacob
cast.who: Patriarch whose era is the second period of laborers.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Sent with Aaron at the midpoint of history to give the law.

cast.name: Aaron
cast.who: Sent with Moses at the midpoint of history under the law.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The only-begotten Son and Word of God, whose coming marks the eleventh hour.

cast.name: John
cast.who: Quoted as saying 'Little children, it is the last hour'; the source does not specify which John, though the quotation matches 1 John.

cast.name: Israel
cast.who: The people to whom the law and the prophets were sent.

cast.name: the thief
cast.who: The repentant criminal crucified with Christ, who received paradise in a single hour.

key_terms.sense: The master of a household, representing God as lord of the world.
The vineyard, representing human nature or the soul.
Laborers hired to work in the vineyard, representing the saints who serve human salvation.
Idle persons standing in the marketplace, representing the Gentiles before Christ.
An hour of the working day, used allegorically for a period of salvation history.
The coming or visitation of Christ, especially his incarnation.
The Gentile nations, as distinct from Israel.
The denarius, the day's wage given equally to all laborers.
The Church, formerly idle but now laboring.
The law given through Moses, illuminating humanity.
The Spirit-bearing prophets sent to Israel.
The yoke of the law borne by Israel.
The burning heat of the day, representing the burden borne under the law.
Paradise, promised to the repentant thief.

scripture: Cyril quotes the Gospel parable from Matthew 20 and alludes to Psalm 18:9 LXX ('the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes') and Psalm 118 LXX ('your commandments are light'), and 1 John 2:18 ('little children, it is the last hour'). Cite as Matthew, Psalms, and 1 John with modern numbering.
uncertain: The precise date of the homily is not stated in the source.
The exact identity of 'John' quoted in hom-rem-mid is not fully specified, though the quotation matches 1 John.
